sections.heading: The idea
sections.figure_alt: A curve of one variable, drawn on labeled axes.
sections.body_md:
The chord definition of convexity does not mention a derivative. When the function is differentiable there is an equivalent picture: every tangent lies under the graph, not only near the point of tangency but at every point of the domain. The linear model built from the value and the gradient is a global underestimator.

This is stronger than a local linear approximation. A smooth nonconvex function still has a tangent, and that tangent is a good approximation nearby, but somewhere else the graph can cross below it. Convexity forbids that crossing.

The inequality also explains minimizers. If the gradient at a point is the zero vector, the underestimator is the constant equal to the function value, so every other point is at least that high. A stationary point of a differentiable convex function is a global minimizer. Strict convexity upgrades that conclusion to a unique minimizer.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
If \(f\) is differentiable on an open convex set, it is convex if and only if every pair of points satisfies
\[
f(y) \ge f(x) + \nabla f(x)^{T} (y - x).
\]
The right-hand side is the first-order Taylor model. The gap \(f(y) - f(x) - \nabla f(x)^{T}(y - x)\) is nonnegative. When the gradient at \(x\) is zero, the inequality says \(f(y) \ge f(x)\) for every \(y\) in the domain.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md: Take \(f(t) = t^2\) at the base point \(5\). The value is \(25\) and the derivative is \(10\). At the comparison point \(8\) the step is \(3\), so the tangent value is 55, equal to \(25 + 30\). The function there is \(64\), and the gap above the tangent is \(9\). The same calculation at the base point itself returns the value \(25\), so the gap is zero on the point of tangency. Moving the comparison point to \(0\) gives the model \(25 + 10\cdot(0 - 5) = -25\), and the function value \(0\) is still above that tangent.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: The inequality runs the opposite way from the chord inequality. The chord says the function is below the secant. The tangent test says the function is above the tangent. Both describe the same bowl. Dropping the gradient term leaves a comparison of function values, which is not the test. A zero gradient without convexity is only a stationary point: it may be a maximum or a saddle. The test needs the gradient at the base point, so it does not apply to a function that merely has directional derivatives along some rays.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: The second-order test replaces this inequality, for a twice differentiable function, by positive semidefiniteness of the Hessian. The first-order inequality is also the reason a descent method can certify optimality: once the gradient is zero, convexity promotes the stationary point to a global solution. On a convex feasible set the same idea becomes a variational inequality, using the gradient only against feasible steps.
